variants.name: std::jthread with std::stop_token (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 absorbs phase 1 and the join into the standard library: std::jthread owns a stop_source, request_stop() is atomic, idempotent and wakes any std::condition_variable_any wait registered with the token, and the thread function polls st.stop_requested() at safe points. Phase 2 - releasing locks, flushing buffers - is still your code after the check, and join() (explicit or via the destructor, which calls request_stop() and join()) publishes completion. The classic atomic-flag form is still justified where the standard floor is C++17 or where the stop must be observed by code that already owns an atomic flag shared with non-thread consumers.
pitfalls: A plain std::condition_variable never observes a stop token; use the std::condition_variable_any overloads that take the token (or notify explicitly), otherwise a sleeping worker ignores request_stop() until its own timeout.

A std::stop_callback runs synchronously on the thread that calls request_stop() and must not throw - an exception escaping it calls std::terminate; keep callbacks short and avoid locks the requester may hold.
Joining from the worker itself (or destroying a jthread member on its own thread) deadlocks: the destructor requests stop and joins, so ownership has to outlive the worker or be released explicitly.
request_stop() returning false means a stop was already requested, not that cleanup has finished: the completion fact is join(), nowhere else.

variants.name: std::thread + atomic flag + condition_variable + join (C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++20 classic keeps the two phases explicit: a std::atomic<bool> (or a protected flag) is the latch, a std::condition_variable is the wake-up, and std::thread::join() is phase 2's completion - as cppreference notes, the thread's completion synchronizes with the successful return from join(). The shared variable must be modified while owning the mutex even when it is atomic, otherwise the notification can be lost. Choose this form when the toolchain is C++11/14/17 or when the same flag must also be readable by a non-thread signal/IO path.
pitfalls: Modifying the flag without the mutex is a lost-wakeup race; the predicate form of wait() (wait(lock, pred)) is the safe idiom because it re-checks after every wake-up.
volatile bool is not a substitute for std::atomic in C++: it gives no inter-thread ordering guarantees (volatile is for unusual memory, not for synchronisation).
A worker that ignores the flag while blocked in I/O (read, accept) never reaches a safe point; close the descriptor (or use non-blocking/fd-aware waiting) as the wake-up mechanism.
